name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Friday 3 February 1984

clue.text: Western sort or shore works

indicators.note: to sort things is to rearrange them into a different order, so the letters that follow get reshuffled

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
opera is the Latin plural of opus, a work

explanation.surface: A Western sort of film, or perhaps some coastal engineering works.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram signal comes before its letters, with 'or' only joining the parts loosely; works as OPERA, the plural of opus, is a favourite crossword trick.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse opera is a jokey name for a cowboy film, a genre also called the Western.

clue.text: Bird takes one as a pain killer

indicators.note: a thing that takes something in holds it inside, so the bird surrounds the next piece

blocks.note: a heron is a long-legged wading bird
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A bird swallows a single painkiller.
explanation.walkthrough: The one goes in after the third letter of the bird, not at either end.
explanation.definitionFit: Heroin is an opiate drug, originally marketed as a medicine to relieve pain.

clue.text: First-class road-holding by Sally?

indicators.note: something holding another keeps it inside its grip, so one piece wraps around the other

blocks.note: Rd is the standard abbreviation for road
A1 means first-class, with the 1 read as the letter I

explanation.surface: A top-quality car's grip on the road, as tested by a driver called Sally.
explanation.walkthrough: Sally looks like a woman's name; with the question mark it is the military sense, a sudden attack from a besieged position.
explanation.definitionFit: A sally is a sortie, a sudden attack out of a defended position, which is a kind of raid.

clue.text: Demonstrative fuse change about five

indicators.note: to change about is to switch things around, so the letters on either side are rearranged together

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An emotional electrician replaces a fuse, maybe around the number five.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Five' looks like the Roman numeral V, but here it is spelt out as fodder: both words together are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A demonstrative person shows feelings openly, and effusive describes gushing, unrestrained expression of feeling.

clue.text: Fireside comfort for two on the slide

blocks.note: a set intended for two, a couple of something
things that slip, read whimsically

explanation.surface: Something cosy by the fire for a couple who keep sliding about.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay is whimsical: a set made for two feet, and things that slip and slide.
explanation.definitionFit: Soft indoor shoes worn by the fire at the end of the day are a classic image of homely comfort.

clue.text: Right for example to read in order to reclassify

indicators.note: putting something in order means rearranging it, so the letters before it are sorted afresh

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for right
e.g. is the abbreviation for 'for example'
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Reading the right examples in sequence so as to sort things into new categories.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In order to' reads as 'so as to', but 'in order' is the anagram signal and the second 'to' joins the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To regrade is to grade again, assigning something to a different class or level.

clue.text: Feast where a man goes on the beer

indicators.note: going on ahead of something means being placed directly before it in the answer

blocks.note: Reg is a common man's name, short for Reginald
ale is a kind of beer

explanation.surface: A party where some fellow goes on a drinking binge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goes on the beer' reads as an idiom for a drinking spree, but it just places the man in front of the beer.
explanation.definitionFit: To regale is to entertain lavishly, to treat someone to a feast.

clue.text: Actors that usually go at the bottom of the bill

definitions.text: usually go at the bottom of the bill
definitions.note: a clause standing for the plural noun: the charges that go there

blocks.note: first meaning: walk-on performers in crowd scenes

blocks.clueFragment: usually go at the bottom of the bill
blocks.note: second meaning: added charges listed last on an invoice

explanation.surface: Bit-part performers who get the lowest billing on a poster.
explanation.walkthrough: The bill looks like a theatre playbill, but the second sense is a restaurant or hotel bill, where additional charges are added last.
explanation.definitionFit: The word covers both non-speaking film performers and additional charges added at the end of an account.

clue.text: Noah, for example, as nautical crossbow-man

blocks.note: first meaning: a sailor from the distant past, as Noah was with his ark
second meaning: the hero of Coleridge's poem, who shot the albatross with his crossbow

explanation.surface: Noah, picturing him as a seafaring archer.
explanation.walkthrough: Coleridge's 'Rime of the Ancient Mariner' has its sailor kill an albatross with a crossbow, bringing a curse on his ship.
explanation.definitionFit: Noah was a very old seafarer, and the phrase is also the title character of Coleridge's famous poem.

clue.text: Violate sporting arena in fine condition

indicators.note: to condition something is to work it into a new shape, so the preceding word is rearranged
one thing placed in another sits inside it, so the arena goes inside the other letters

blocks.note: a boxing ring is a sporting arena
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Breaking the rules by keeping a sports ground in good shape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In fine condition' reads as 'in good shape', but 'condition' tells you to rearrange the letters of fine, and the ring goes inside them.
explanation.definitionFit: To infringe a law or right is to violate or break it.

clue.text: Plastered cuts on American college-girl

blocks.note: taken as written, then turned round
a co-ed is an American term for a female student at a mixed college

explanation.surface: A drunk American student keeps getting into cuts.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no word telling you to turn the first word round; the solver must spot it from the needed letters. 'Plastered' looks like slang for drunk but means covered in plaster.
explanation.definitionFit: Stucco is a fine plaster for walls, so a stuccoed wall has been plastered.

clue.text: Quiet perhaps for a trumpet

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the words are only a possible arrangement, so their letters may be shuffled

blocks.note: sh is the sound used to ask for quiet
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Is a quiet tone perhaps good for a trumpet?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps for a' reads like plain English, but the two little words are the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A shofar is the ancient Jewish ram's-horn instrument blown like a trumpet at Rosh Hashanah.

clue.text: Right one to lament about a mother?

definitions.note: an adjective, 'like a mother', defined by a noun phrase with a question mark

indicators.note: about can mean turned around or scattered, so the letters before it are moved into a new order

blocks.note: R is the usual abbreviation for right
a means one
taken as written

explanation.surface: Is a mother just the right person to mourn about something?
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the definition is loose: the answer describes what is characteristic of a mother.
explanation.definitionFit: Maternal means motherly, of or like a mother, so the answer is the quality the definition points to.

clue.text: Marks that show where the fighting was

definitions.note: a clause where the answer is a plural noun: the things that show this

blocks.note: first meaning: drawn strokes
second meaning: the front positions of opposing armies

explanation.surface: Scars that reveal where a brawl took place.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests scars or bruises; the second sense is military, the fronts where armies faced each other.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means strokes drawn with a pen and also the battle fronts where armies are positioned.

clue.text: Took shares in being surrounded

definitions.note: the answer is a past participle; 'being surrounded' matches it in a passive sense

blocks.note: first meaning: put money into a company
second meaning: besieged

explanation.surface: A shareholder's anxious sense of being hemmed in by investments.
explanation.walkthrough: The military sense is old: to invest a fortress is to surround and blockade it.
explanation.definitionFit: Invest means both to put money into shares and, in military language, to lay siege to a place.

clue.text: Spring in hair is seen as sin

indicators.note: one thing placed in another sits inside it, so the first piece goes inside the second

blocks.note: a tress is a long lock of hair
a spa is a mineral spring

explanation.surface: A bounce in one's hairstyle is regarded as sinful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spring' suggests bounce in the hair, but it is a mineral spring, which goes between the third and fourth letters of the lock.
explanation.definitionFit: Trespass is an old word for sin or wrongdoing, as in the Lord's Prayer's 'forgive us our trespasses'.

clue.text: Fellowship in trade

blocks.note: first meaning: social dealings and companionship, an older sense
second meaning: the buying and selling of goods

explanation.walkthrough: The first meaning is dated: commerce once meant social intercourse or fellowship between people.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means buying and selling in business, and in older English also meant friendly social dealings.

clue.text: Ring Peter about one at work?

definitions.note: a verb, to work or function, defined loosely by a phrase with a question mark

indicators.note: about suggests moving things around, so the name and the one are rearranged

blocks.note: a ring is round, like the letter O
taken as written
a means one

explanation.surface: Phone Peter about someone who is at their job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ring' reads as phoning someone, but it is the round letter. The definition is loose: to operate is to be at work, functioning.
explanation.definitionFit: A machine or surgeon that operates is functioning or working, so being at work is the sense.

clue.text: Hard cut to point

blocks.note: to sever is to cut off
E, east, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: A harsh cut right to the point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Point' here is a compass point, a standard crossword source of N, S, E or W.
explanation.definitionFit: Severe means harsh or stern, and a hard winter or hard punishment is a severe one.

clue.text: Misgivings in small quantities

blocks.note: first meaning: moral doubts or hesitation
second meaning: old apothecaries' weights of twenty grains

explanation.surface: Having small doubts in small amounts.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense comes from the apothecaries' scruple, a tiny unit of weight, and from there any very small amount.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means moral qualms, and also tiny measures from the old apothecaries' weight system.

clue.text: Keep service spirit up with a lottery

indicators.note: keep here means hold beside, so one piece is kept right next to the other
in a down answer, going up means reading the word from bottom to top

blocks.note: the RAF, Royal Air Force, is one of the British armed services
an elf is a sprite or spirit

explanation.surface: Raising servicemen's morale by running a lottery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keep spirits up' is the idiom the surface plays on; 'Keep' only loosely joins the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A raffle is a lottery in which tickets are drawn for prizes.

clue.text: Suit man with practical skills

blocks.note: he is the pronoun for a man
arts as crafts, skills learned by practice

explanation.surface: A tailor, the man who makes a suit, has hands-on skills.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suit' suggests clothes and a tailor, but it is a suit of playing cards.
explanation.definitionFit: Hearts is one of the four suits in a pack of playing cards.

clue.text: Don't get upset, fees may be mitigated

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over and thrown into disorder, so the letters around it are mixed up

blocks.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped
taken as written

explanation.surface: Reassurance to a client: stay calm, the charges might be reduced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Don't get upset' reads as soothing advice, but the indicator sits between its two pieces of fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: To mitigate a blow or penalty is to make it less severe, that is, to soften it.

clue.text: Porch may show way round one

blocks.note: St, street, is a way
O is round in shape
a means one

explanation.surface: A porch can show the path round to the house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round' looks like a direction, but it is the round letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A stoa is a covered colonnade or portico in Greek architecture, a kind of porch.

clue.text: A large proportion leave after cock-fight

indicators.note: after places the word before it behind the one that follows in the answer

blocks.note: a main is an old term for a cockfighting match
to part is to leave or go away

explanation.surface: Most of the spectators walk out after a cockfight.
explanation.walkthrough: A main is a set of matches in cockfighting, an old sporting term that crosswords still use.
explanation.definitionFit: The main part of something is the bulk of it, a large proportion of the whole.

clue.text: Girls that may be sweet on the doctor

blocks.clueFragment: Girls that may be sweet on the doctor
blocks.note: surface reading: young women who have a crush on their physician
setter's reading: put MO, the medical officer, in front of the answer and you get a dark sugar syrup

explanation.surface: Young women who fancy their doctor.
explanation.walkthrough: Sweet on means infatuated with, but here it means becoming a sweet syrup when the doctor goes on top; MO, medical officer, is the usual crossword doctor.
explanation.definitionFit: Lasses is a northern British and Scottish word for girls or young women.

clue.text: Flower that proves there's a sea

indicators.note: dough that proves swells and changes its shape, so the words after it take a new form

blocks.note: all ten letters, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A seaside plant whose presence is evidence of the nearby ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Proves' looks like 'demonstrates', but it is meant in the baker's sense of rising and changing.
explanation.definitionFit: Heartsease is the wild pansy, a small purple and yellow flower.
